title: Every season of a Jewish life
hook: Jewish tradition marks every stage from birth to death
carry: each season of life is marked and blessed

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was character is daily: one small act, repeated. Today a new block begins: the life cycle.

Pencil lines climb a kitchen doorframe. Each one has a name and a date beside it, scratched in on a birthday or the first day of school. Some families do this without being told to. They want to mark the moments when a life moves up a notch, so they don't slip by unnoticed. Judaism has its own doorframe, and it runs from a life's first days to its last, and beyond. Before stopping at any one mark, a look at the whole frame.
screen: `PENCIL LINES ON A DOORFRAME.` → `MARKING THE MOMENTS.` → `THE WHOLE FRAME.`

segments.voice: First, the seasons. Ecclesiastes says: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." And then: "A time to be born, and a time to die." The tradition takes the seasons of a life seriously enough to give each one a ritual. Second, the marks. A new baby is welcomed with blessings and a name; for boys, with a covenant ceremony, the brit milah. A young person comes of age as a bar or bat mitzvah, a son or daughter of the commandments. Two people marry under a canopy, the chuppah. And at the end there are rituals for dying, for burial, and for the mourners who stay behind: days of sitting at home, called shiva, and the words of the kaddish. Third, a map in the Mishnah. In Ethics of the Fathers, Judah ben Tema lays out a life by ages: at five, scripture; at ten, Mishnah; at thirteen, the commandments; at eighteen, the wedding canopy; and on, through strength, understanding and counsel, to old age. It isn't a schedule anyone must keep. It's a picture of a life with stages, each with its own work. Fourth, one blessing for many doorways. Jewish tradition has a short blessing called shehecheyanu, said at new and joyful moments: a first fruit of the season, a holiday's first night, a new home, a new garment. It thanks God for keeping us alive and bringing us to this time. The rituals don't make the moments happen. They make sure a person stops, and notices, that they have.
screen: `A SEASON FOR EVERY THING.` · `BIRTH, COMING OF AGE, CANOPY, MOURNING.` · `A LIFE BY AGES.` · `A BLESSING FOR NEW MOMENTS.` · then, large: `A LIFE HAS RITUALS.`

segments.voice: Start at the beginning of your own life, as far back as you know: a naming, a blessing, a party, a photo, then a birthday that mattered, a graduation, a first job, a move, a wedding, a funeral you stood at. Let each mark come up like a pencil line on the doorframe, and notice which ones had a ritual and which passed with nothing to mark them. Notice, too, the next doorway ahead of you.
A life has rituals: birth, coming of age, marriage, mourning, each stage marked, and one blessing for the new moments in between. Today's word.
Your line: each season of life is marked and blessed, from the first days to the last. Go gently.

howItsDone: Jewish life-cycle rituals are usually led by family and community together: a baby's naming in the synagogue or at home, a bar or bat mitzvah's first reading from the Torah, a wedding under the chuppah, and shiva, when mourners receive visitors at home.
